fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more interesting questions, because people sometimes say, well, humans learn quickly because evolution gave us a really good prior. And for some things that's clearly true. Like vision, locomotion, recognizing faces, social stuff, evolution had a very long time to work on those. So maybe it's not surprising that a kid can do those things without much data.

But then you look at language, math, coding. Math is pretty recent. Coding is extremely recent, it's like 70 years old. There's no way evolution had time to build a prior that says, here is how you write a for loop. And yet people learn to code, some people learn it quite well, and they do it with a very, very small amount of data compared to what we use to train these models. A person who becomes a decent programmer has seen, I don't know, some number of textbooks, some number of examples, a few years of practice. It's nothing. It's a tiny fraction of what's on the internet.

So I think what that tells you is that the thing which makes humans good learners is not a bunch of narrow priors. It's something more general. There's some general-purpose machinery that can take a domain evolution never saw and still learn it efficiently, robustly, from few examples. And I'd say the robustness part is maybe the more important part. Humans aren't that good at math, honestly. Most people are quite bad at it. But when a person learns something, they tend to not have these weird failure modes where they're great at one thing and then fall apart on something that's basically the same thing. Their understanding is kind of continuous.

And I think it's worth being a little humble here and saying, we don't know what that machinery is. We know it exists, because we see it. And I think it's very likely that it has an ML analog, that there is a principle, a fairly simple one probably, that we just haven't found yet. That's actually one of the reasons I think there is still real research to be done, and it's not just scaling.

r001.rationale: The response says humans learn recent domains like coding despite lacking an evolved domain-specific prior, pointing instead to general-purpose learning machinery.

opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting things to think about. Humans learn these things with very little data compared to our models, and they learn them in a much more robust way. Somebody can become a pretty good programmer or a pretty good mathematician after a relatively small amount of practice, and once they've learned it, they really understand it. They don't fall apart the moment you step slightly outside of what they've seen.

You could say, well, maybe that's because evolution gave us a lot of useful prior knowledge. And for some things, I think that's quite plausible. Vision, locomotion, dexterity. Our ancestors needed those for hundreds of millions of years, so it's reasonable that evolution baked in something very good there. When you see how well a person can move through the world, maybe a big part of that is a prior.

But language, math, and coding are different. Language is fairly recent on evolutionary timescales, and math and coding are extremely recent. There hasn't been time for evolution to give us some special prior for writing proofs or debugging code. And yet people are still very good at learning them, and they learn them with a sample efficiency and reliability that our models don't come close to. That suggests to me that it's not mainly about the prior. It suggests that people have something more fundamental: a better learning algorithm, a better way of generalizing.

One more thing stands out to me. When a person is learning, they're not relying on someone giving them a carefully specified reward for every step. A teenager learning to drive, or a student working on a math problem, has an internal sense of whether things are going well. They can tell when they're confused, when they're on the right track, when something feels off, and they correct themselves continuously. That's an internal value function, and it's very robust. It works in so many situations it was never explicitly trained for.

So human learning in these domains says to me that there's a principle of learning and generalization we haven't fully captured yet. Our models are very capable, but they generalize dramatically worse than people do. I think understanding that gap is one of the most important questions there is.

r001.rationale: The response says language, math, and coding are too recent for evolution to have supplied specialized priors, and concludes that human performance points to a more fundamental learning ability: a better learning algorithm and way of generalizing.

fable-5.text:
You know, I think it's an interesting question because you could argue that language, math, and coding — they're not the same, actually, in what they tell us. Let me explain what I mean.

Language is something that every human being learns, and learns extremely robustly. Small children learn language from an amount of data that is tiny by the standards of our models, and they do it reliably. You could say that evolution has prepared us for language, in some sense. The machinery is there. So maybe language is less informative about learning in general, because there's so much prior built in.

But math and coding are different. Evolution did not prepare us for math and coding. These are very recent things on an evolutionary timescale. And yet some people learn them — and the way they learn them is very interesting. A person who becomes good at math or at programming does not do so by seeing millions of examples. They see a comparatively small number of examples, they practice, and then they generalize very far beyond what they've seen. And what's more, their learning is robust. If a person learns to code, they don't make the kind of strange, brittle mistakes where they're superhuman in one narrow situation and then completely fall apart in a slightly different one. Human competence is much smoother than that.

So what does this suggest? I think it suggests that humans have some kind of general-purpose learning ability — a much better "machine learning," if you want to call it that — that is not about having pretrained on enormous amounts of data for that particular skill. The teenager who learns to drive a car in ten hours is doing something similar. It's unsupervised in a sense, it's sample-efficient, and it's robust. And the fact that there's variation between people — that some people pick these things up much faster — tells you that whatever this ability is, it's a real, concrete thing. It's not magic. It's some principle that brains implement.

And I find that encouraging, actually, because if it's a principle, it can be understood. The gap between how our models learn and how people learn — the huge difference in sample efficiency, the robustness — that gap is pointing at something. It's telling us that there is a better way of doing learning that we haven't found yet, and the human example is the proof that it exists.

r001.rationale: The response says language may be less informative because humans have substantial built-in preparation, while robust, sample-efficient learning in math and coding points to a general-purpose learning ability implemented by the brain. It presents this as an underlying principle rather than a complicated prior.

opus-5.text:
I think the most striking thing is just how little it takes. A person who becomes good at math does not do it by reading the entire internet. A teenager learns to drive in ten hours of practice, and after that they're a pretty reliable driver. So whatever the human learning algorithm is, it's dramatically more data-efficient than what we do, and I don't think we have a good account of why.

The other thing that I find suggestive is the transfer. If a person spends a few years doing serious math, they don't just get better at math — they get better at thinking about things that aren't math at all. They become harder to fool. Something general improved. Whereas with our models, if you train hard on competitive programming, you get a system that is spectacular at competitive programming and that's roughly what you get. So humans seem to be extracting something more abstract from the same experience, and I think that gap is where the real remaining question lives.

And then there's the question of what distinguishes the people who learn well from the people who don't, which to me doesn't look mostly like raw processing speed. It looks like something closer to taste — knowing which problem is worth attacking, noticing the moment when you're confused instead of gliding past it, having a feel for when an explanation is actually load-bearing versus when you've just memorized a chain of words. That's a kind of value function, and it's doing an enormous amount of work, because it determines what you choose to spend your learning on.

What gives me hope is that it can't be that complicated. The genome is small. Evolution did not have room to specify very much about how your cortex learns language or math — those are far too recent. So there's some relatively simple principle there that we haven't found yet, rather than ten thousand special-purpose mechanisms. I think that principle is findable.

r001.rationale: The response argues that human learning ability comes from a relatively simple, undiscovered principle, not many special-purpose mechanisms.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the interesting thing about those three is that they're recent. Evolution had a long time to prepare us for vision, locomotion, and maybe for some social and emotional things. But math and coding barely existed a moment ago, on an evolutionary timescale. Language is a bit older, but it's still not something we had millions of years to refine. So it's hard to argue that people are good at these because evolution baked in the answers. It suggests that what makes people good learners is more general than a prior for a particular domain.

What stands out to me is how little data it takes. A person picks up a new area of math from a few examples and a bit of struggle. A person learns to program after a modest amount of practice. The models need vastly more, and they're still less reliable in a way that's hard to pin down. So whatever people are doing, it isn't just absorbing statistics. The learning is much more efficient and much more robust.

The other thing I'd point to is that people don't need someone standing over them with a precise reward signal at every step. A student working through a textbook alone has a sense of whether they understand something. They can tell when a proof doesn't feel right, or when their code is probably wrong before they've run it. That internal sense of "this is going well" or "this is off" lets them correct themselves and keep going without constant outside supervision. I think that's a big part of being good at learning: you have a built-in way of evaluating your own understanding, so you can learn from a very small amount of experience.

So my takeaway is that there's some underlying principle of learning that people have and that we haven't captured yet. It isn't specific to language or math or code, and it works in all of them. I don't think I can say exactly what it is, but I'm confident it exists. I also think that figuring out how to get that kind of generalization and sample efficiency is one of the most important questions in the field.

r001.rationale: The response says these recent domains are unlikely to be learned through evolution-baked, domain-specific priors and points instead to an underlying general principle of human learning.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the most striking thing is how little data people need. A child hears a limited amount of speech before producing sentences that make sense, and someone can pick up a new programming language from a handful of examples and some trial and error. That's very different from how we train models, which need enormous amounts of text to reach something comparable.

So I don't think what makes people good learners is mainly how much they've absorbed. It's the quality of the internal model they build. Good learners don't just memorize surface patterns. They find the underlying structure, like the grammar behind the sentences or the principle behind the proof, and that structure lets them handle cases they've never seen. They also keep a tight loop with reality: they try something, notice when it's wrong, and update in a targeted way.

If I had to put it in one line, it's compression with understanding. The fastest learners can take a small number of experiences and extract the right abstraction from them. I think that's still the piece we don't fully know how to build into machines.

r001.rationale: The response points to structure extraction and internal models as sources of learning ability, but it contrasts these with absorbing more data—not with relying primarily on a complicated prior. That part of the criterion is not communicated.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think math and coding are particularly interesting because you can ask: where does our ability to learn these things come from? With language, you could imagine that evolution gave us something quite specialized. But programming is too recent for that explanation to work directly.

So that suggests that whatever makes people good at learning is fairly general. We have some ability to discover structure, to form abstractions, and then to use those abstractions in a new situation. And this ability can apply to things very different from the situations that originally produced it.

There’s also a distinction between remembering what you’ve seen and understanding something well enough that its consequences become clear. In math, you might struggle with a concept, and then something clicks. Now a whole collection of problems becomes easier. That seems like an important property of learning: an experience can change how you interpret many other experiences.

To me, the question is: what kind of learning process makes that possible, and makes it happen reliably?

r001.rationale: The response argues that coding is too recent to be explained by an evolved specialization and infers a general human capacity to discover structure and form abstractions. This points to a broad source of learning ability rather than primarily to a complicated prior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most striking thing is how well people generalize. You explain something to a person, they work through a few examples, and sometimes they get it. They can then use the idea in a situation that looks quite different from the examples. Of course, sometimes they don’t get it, and there are very large differences between people. But the fact that this is possible is interesting.

With language, you can say, well, evolution has prepared us to learn language. That seems like a reasonable explanation for some of our ability. But mathematics and programming are more puzzling. Evolution didn’t have much opportunity to prepare us specifically for writing computer programs. And yet people can become very good at it.

So that suggests that evolution found something more general—a way of learning that can be applied to things that weren’t present in the environment where we evolved.

Then the question is: what is that thing? What lets you take relatively little experience and extract something useful from it? I think that’s a very important question. Saying that humans have a lot of prior knowledge is part of an explanation, but you still need to explain why that knowledge transfers so effectively to a new domain.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution found a more general way of learning that transfers to domains like mathematics and programming, and questions whether prior knowledge alone explains that transfer.

sol-6.text: I think the striking thing is that people don’t learn language, math, and coding in exactly the same way, but there’s a common pattern. We build a mental model, try to use it, notice where it fails, and revise it. In language, the feedback is often social; in math, it’s whether the argument works; in coding, the program either does what you intended or it doesn’t. So being good at learning seems to involve more than absorbing examples. It involves finding useful structure in them and being able to correct your understanding when reality pushes back.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shared pattern of building and revising mental models, but it does not identify this as a fundamental source of learning ability or contrast it with a complicated prior.

terra-5.6.text: I think the main lesson is that learning is a very general capability. People who are good at learning tend to be good across language, math, coding, and lots of other domains—not because they have a separate specialized mechanism for each one, but because they can build good internal representations, notice patterns, and update from feedback. The details matter, of course, but there’s a deep commonality underneath.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general learning capability shared across domains, but it does not communicate the contrast with a complicated prior.

sol-5.6.text: I think it suggests that what matters is not simply the amount of data, but having the right internal structure and learning signals. Humans learn from relatively few examples because they bring strong prior knowledge, curiosity, and an ability to connect new ideas to what they already understand. In language, math, and coding, the best learners seem to build compact mental models—they do not merely memorize procedures. They practice, notice errors, and reorganize their understanding. So perhaps being good at learning means being able to extract the underlying structure of a problem and to generate useful feedback for yourself.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes internal structure, learning signals, and self-generated feedback, but it does not clearly present these as a fundamental source of learning ability in contrast to relying primarily on a complicated prior. It also cites strong prior knowledge as a factor.

luna-5.6.text: I think the main thing is that humans are extremely good at finding abstractions and reusing them. You don’t learn every sentence, mathematical fact, or line of code independently—you discover underlying structure, and then that structure lets you generalize to new situations. Humans also learn actively: they ask questions, form hypotheses, experiment, and seek out information that resolves their uncertainty. And all of this is built on very strong prior knowledge from evolution, development, and culture. So learning is not just absorbing data; it’s combining rich priors with experience to build increasingly powerful, compositional models of the world.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes abstraction and reuse, but also presents strong prior knowledge as a key part of learning. It does not clearly say that learning ability comes from a fundamental source rather than primarily from a complicated prior.

luna-6.text:
I think it suggests that good learning is largely about finding the structure underneath the examples. Language, math, and coding look very different on the surface, but in each case you’re learning patterns, building abstractions, and then reusing them in situations you haven’t seen before. The learner who can connect a new idea to what they already understand has a big advantage.

And people don’t learn in a vacuum. We come with prior expectations, we get feedback from the world, and we can ask questions or try things out. So being good at learning isn’t just absorbing lots of information. It’s noticing what matters, testing your understanding, and being willing to revise it when it doesn’t work.

r001.rationale: The response says good learning is largely about finding structure beneath examples, building abstractions, and reusing them. Prior expectations are mentioned, but the response presents them as one part of learning rather than its primary source.
